title: Beneath a Wyoming coal town's last smokestack, 345 megawatts of liquid metal just broke ...
description:
The grid infrastructure was already in place, the skilled workforce was already here, and a community that understood energy work would not need years of convincing.
A coal town that knew what was coming Kemmerer, Wyoming has lived on energy work for generations.
When the Naughton coal plant next door began its wind down, the town did not panic.
The grid infrastructure was already in place, the skilled workforce was already here, and a community that understood energy work would not need years of convincing.
On the Wyoming plateau where a coal plant’s final years are ticking down, the concrete is already setting.
text:
Something unusual is rising in a small Wyoming coal town, and at first glance it looks like every industrial project that came before it.

There are concrete foundations being poured.

There are steel frameworks going up against a pale sky.

The grid infrastructure was already in place, the skilled workforce was already here, and a community that understood energy work would not need years of convincing.

The hills around Kemmerer have absorbed the noise of heavy industry for more than a century, and the crews working the site have not changed much either.

But what is being built here has never been built anywhere in America before.

And the number that will define it is only half the story.

A coal town that knew what was coming

Kemmerer, Wyoming has lived on energy work for generations.

Its workforce learned boilers, turbines, and high voltage lines before most of them finished high school.

When the Naughton coal plant next door began its wind down, the town did not panic.

It had been through transitions before.

What nobody expected was the specific thing that would arrive to replace it.

The grid infrastructure was already in place, the skilled workforce was already here, and a community that understood energy work would not need years of convincing.

The permit that took fifty years to arrive

Before a single foundation could be poured for the reactor itself, a piece of paper had to exist that had never existed before.

In March 2026, the NRC issued a construction permit for the project, the first ever granted by the commission for a commercial non light water reactor.

Every commercial reactor operating in the United States today runs on ordinary pressurized water.

Approving something fundamentally different meant the regulator had to build an entirely new review framework from scratch.

The NRC review finished in 18 months, nine months ahead of schedule.

Then, on April 23, 2026, construction officially began.

The metal that melts like butter and runs hotter than a furnace

Most reactors you have ever heard of use water, but water has a problem.

To stop it from turning to steam inside the core, engineers must keep it under crushing pressure, roughly 155 times the air pressure at sea level.

This reactor circulates liquid sodium coolant through its core, where the sodium absorbs heat generated by nuclear fission in the fuel assemblies.

Liquid sodium runs near normal air pressure and can carry enormous heat without the thick walled pressure vessel that makes conventional plants so costly.

The reactor’s heat output exceeds 500 degrees Celsius.

That is hot enough to do something conventional plants cannot quite manage, something grid operators across the country have been waiting a long time to see.

The tank that turns a reactor into a battery

Here is what the project is really about.

The plant pairs a 345 MW sodium cooled fast reactor with an integrated molten salt energy storage system, and on April 23, 2026, construction began in earnest.

When electricity demand is low, surplus heat from the reactor is pumped into a massive tank of molten salt, a mineral mixture that holds heat the way a cast iron skillet holds warmth long after the burner goes off.

When demand spikes, that stored heat is released back through the turbines.

The storage system can boost output to anywhere between 100 and 500 megawatts for more than 5.5 hours, ramping at 10 percent per minute.

At its 500 megawatt peak, that covers something close to 400,000 homes.

A nuclear plant that can sprint when the grid screams for power, then settle back to a steady baseload hum, is something no architect of the American grid ever had available before.

For Wyoming’s coal communities, the arrival of a technology this flexible carries its own particular weight.

What comes next, and what could still go wrong

The energy storage island is proceeding ahead of the nuclear island, with construction completion expected in early 2031.

That sequencing is deliberate: the two halves are designed to be built and licensed on independent schedules, reducing the risk of one delay cascading into the whole project.

The total project cost is close to four billion dollars, with roughly half coming from the Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program.

HALEU supply, the specialized high assay low enriched uranium the reactor requires, remains the program’s principal watch item.

The NRC’s transportation rules will also shape how quickly the fuel supply chain can be assembled.

Around 1,600 construction workers will be mobilized at peak building activity, with about 250 permanent jobs expected once the plant is operational.

Many of those roles match the exact skills a coal or gas crew already carries.

On the Wyoming plateau where a coal plant’s final years are ticking down, the concrete is already setting.

It is being built, right now, on the same road they have always driven to work.

It Started With a Waiver

California has the biggest market for cars among the 50 states of the U.S. You could say that U.S. market vehicles are built for Californian standards first, then the rest of the country later, which is a big point of friction for many automakers. The strictest emissions rules in the U.S. can be found in California, which was brought about by a waiver granted to the state under the Clean Air Act. However, all of that might change soon, if lawmakers get their way.

Four U.S. Senators, Wyoming's Cynthia Lummis, Missouri's Eric Schmitt, Nebraska's Pete Ricketts, and Ohio's Jon Husted, are leading the effort to remove the waiver issued by the federal government to the state of California that allowed it to impose stricter emissions regulations in the first place. These senators now want to take that permission away, but a majority vote is needed for that to happen.

In order to get California's waiver repealed, a majority vote is required, which is less than the 60 that's typically required under normal circumstances. This ruling follows the Congressional Review Act (CRA).

California Laws Are Affecting Other States

From an automaker's perspective, conquering California is the first step, and then the rest of the 47 mainland States will follow. Logistics will be tough for Alaska and Hawaii, though, but I digress. Automakers build for California first, getting the biggest hurdle out of the way first, which forces the other U.S. States to adopt similar rules.

Back in June, the Environmental Protection Agency submitted the California waivers to Congress for a possible repeal. GM Authority picked up a Reuters report stating that the waivers are to be submitted to Congress under the CRA by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

Historically, President Trump has also called for executive orders, congressional reviews, and federal lawsuits in a bid to block California's self-imposed emissions rules since his first term in office. Federal emissions standards have also been eased for internal combustion vehicles during his term, but California remains strict.

If you want to buy an electric vehicle, California is one of the best places to do it. The state is the most pro-EV state in the U.S. right now because getting around with battery power doesn't pay attention to the emissions laws. The state government also put in a bid to axe the sale of all new gasoline-powered vehicles by 2035, which was rescinded by Congress in 2025.

California Sues Back

The state filed a federal lawsuit, claiming that the EPA's action of sending the waivers to the Senate for consideration under the CRA was illegal. The four senators pushing for this contended that California's emissions regulations affect other states.

Because California is the largest market for cars in the U.S., and because manufacturers have a big incentive to follow California's regulations, other states have no choice but to follow. Essentially, because of California's federal waiver, everyone's forced to follow the strictest of its regulations that cover commercial trucks, passenger vehicles, and even down to off-road vehicles and equipment like lawnmowers and other machines that run on fossil fuels.

If California were to keep its federal waiver, it's possible that the State will continue to hold a massive influence over the direction of the rest of the U.S. auto industry. However, if the waiver were to be repealed, the rest of the 49 states would have a more equal say in what passes and what doesn't.

text:
Gov. Greg Abbott has moved to temporarily halt new data centers from connecting to Texas’ power grid unless companies first provide the state with detailed information about their expected electricity and water use, a step that has drawn criticism from President Donald Trump.

In an interview with Punchbowl News, Trump said Abbott’s new moratorium is “a mistake.” Trump added, “I’m not taking position. I just think a mistake...When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”

On Monday, Abbott paused approvals for any data center seeking to connect to the state’s power grid, citing reliability concerns. Abbott’s office said ERCOT is tracking a more than 500% increase in peak electricity demand.

Under the moratorium, companies must share information with the state about a proposed facility’s electricity and water use. If a company does not meet the governor’s requirements, the data center will be kept off the grid.

In a statement from the governor’s office, officials said in part: “Simply put Texans must come first.”

Josh Blank, Research Director with the Texas Politics Project, said the disagreement places Abbott in a difficult political position within his party.

“It forces the Republican Governor of Texas to take what can be seen as an anti-development or anti-business position, even though at this point it’s just trying to sort of get a rein in on this issue of data centers,” Blank said.

Blank also pointed to public opinion as the November election approaches.

“A June UT Texas Politics Project polling showed a majority of Texas voters opposed to the construction of data centers in their community,” he said.

RELATED: Trump calls Texas' data center opposition a "mistake"

The Texas Data Center Map shows 536 facilities statewide, including 66 in Austin.

Despite Trump’s criticism, Blank said Abbott is likely to stick with his decision.

“Governor Abbott is very well-informed when it comes to the views of Texans, and his decisions about data centers and the movements he’s made so far reflect a deep understanding of what the politics of this look like,” Blank said.

So far, there has been no indication Abbott plans to change course following the president’s criticism.

text:
Story Produced by the Concord Monitor, a Member of

CONCORD, NH – It seems increasingly likely that New Hampshire drivers who have scraped the inspection decal off their car windshields won’t have to replace it.

The Environmental Protection Agency said Thursday it is proposing to speed up actions that would legalize New Hampshire’s decision last January to end the state’s car-inspection program.

That’s not necessarily the end of the story, since a Wilton woman has sued over the end of the car inspections, citing air pollution and its effect on people’s breathing, a lawsuit that has drawn support from the manufacturer of the equipment used in those inspections. But odds are that New Hampshire lawmakers’ decision to end the state program, despite violating federal law, will stick.

This week, the EPA proposed to grant New Hampshire’s petition to withdraw from the Ozone Transport Region and to approve the state’s request to remove its Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance program from the State Implementation Plan.

The move would speed up the process, which normally can take 18 months. If it goes through, New Hampshire would no longer be in violation of the Clean Air Act.

The Ozone Transport Region, which covers most of the Northeast, was established under the Clean Air Act to reduce ground-level ozone, a major pollutant, through inspections of vehicle exhaust. The State Implementation Plan is an overarching program to ensure that states met air quality standards under the federal act.

Last year, the state legislature and Gov. Kelly Ayotte passed a law ending annual car inspections as of January 2026 without getting EPA permission to back out of the Clear Air Act requirements. That led to a lawsuit from Kentucky-based company Gordon-Darby, which makes the inspection equipment. The company has since dropped its suit.

SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- If you've been thinking about switching to an electric vehicle, California is offering a new tax incentive.

Gov. Gavin Newsom just announced drivers can now get thousands of dollars off when they buy a new EV for the first time.

The fine print is that this applies to new cars under $50,000 and used cars under $25,000. Currently, this applies to EVs made by Hyundai, Tesla, Lucid, and will soon include Ford, Rivian, Chevrolet, Kia and even more carmakers this fall.

Car sales pitch aside, Newsom says this is all about California being a global clean energy leader as the Trump administration has backed away from several emissions goals, which Americans have mixed opinions about.

MORE: Gov. Newsom announces $1 billion rebate program for electric trucks

Elon Graham loves zooming around in his wife's car, which is fittingly a Tesla.

"I love the car. The car is great. All the functions, all the things it does," Graham said.

But what he doesn't love is the charging time.

"In my line of work, I just have a lot of driving to do, and in just an eight-hour shift. I don't have time to stop and charge," Graham said.

It's a big reason why he hasn't made the switch from his own gas car. Those hesitancies are exactly what California is hoping to overcome.

Now, Californians will automatically get a $3,500 tax credit for a new zero-emission car, or half that for a used EV.

.

The state set aside just over $135 million as a one-time investment, with partnering automakers matching that amount.

"It means cleaner air for their children. It means lower fuel and maintenance costs, saving money each month for the family budget," said California Air Resources Board Chair Lauren Sanchez.

It's part of a pledge Newsom made before President Donald Trump took office for a second term, ending the $7,500 federal EV rebates.

"The United States is doubling down on stupid. We're trying in California to maintain our dominance in this space," Newsom said.

A July PPIC survey found roughly two-thirds of Californians oppose Newsom's ban on the sale of gas-powered cars by 2035. His response?

MORE: Trump administration sues California over state's nation-leading vehicle-emission rules

"This is the next global race for the United States of America that cares about manufacturing, jobs, the industrial economy. They care about blue-collar workers. What the hell is wrong with us," Newsom said.

Drivers like Graham aren't far from getting on board but are hoping an electric future is as easy as a petroleum present.

"If we can figure out how to charge it faster, I don't think there would be anything wrong with this at all," he said.

So as for those charging stations, California has more than 216,000 EV public and shared private charging ports -- which is behind the state's goal -- but Newsom noted that does not include private charging in your garage, for example.

And Newsom also announced the state just surpassed 21,000 megawatts in its battery storage systems, which is powered by solar. That's enough to power nearly 16 million California homes for hours after sundown.

Nevertheless, since the March 2011 nuclear disaster in northeastern Japan, geothermal energy has still been regarded as the "last frontier" of renewable energy, according to a Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry official.
text:
As concerns in Japan continue to mount over the impact of high crude oil prices on energy costs, one country has effectively harnessed its own geothermal resources, creating a contrasting energy landscape.

That country is Iceland, known for its volcanoes and high cost of living, where a simple order of bread and coffee at a cafe can easily cost over 2,000 yen. But unlike Japan, another volcanic island nation, utility costs there are kept low thanks to its abundant renewable energy resources.

About a 30-minute drive from the capital, Reykjavik, pipelines run across the barren landscape. This infrastructure delivers hot water directly from geothermal power plants to individual households. Nearly all of Iceland's electricity is generated from hydropower and geothermal energy.

Hydropower accounts for about 70 percent of the country's electricity, while geothermal energy provides the remainder and plays a key role in supplying heating and hot water.

Renewable energy makes up about 85 percent of energy consumption, excluding transportation and other sources.

"Low utility bills are a lifesaver for our household budget," says Megumi Nishida, a resident of Reykjavik originally from Japan.

The Nishida family of three lives in an 80-year-old detached house. Their January utility bill, covering electricity and hot water for 24-hour heating, came to about 21,000 yen.

"It would be even cheaper for us in a new, energy-efficient home (here in Iceland)," says Nishida.

Iceland seems affordable considering the high cost of living and utilities during the equally cold winters in Hokkaido, northern Japan. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, utilities cost around 30,000 to 40,000 yen per month in 2025, depending on the heating infrastructure.

Electric vehicles are a common sight in Reykjavik, and charging stations are everywhere. Iceland relies on imports for gasoline and it remains expensive, but electricity is very cheap, which is why EVs have become so widespread.

At least one Japanese entrepreneur is taking advantage of Iceland's low energy costs for his agriculture business. Kenichi Noda decided to cultivate premium Japanese strawberries such as Beni Hoppe because of Iceland's low-cost geothermal energy, clean water and stable renewable electricity.

Noda is chief executive officer of the start-up iFarm Iceland located at the Iceland Eco-Business Park near the renowned Blue Lagoon geothermal spa.

Although daylight hours are short and winters are harsh, he operates an underground climate-controlled vertical farm around the clock using LED lighting and geothermal heating. Because of the optimal growing conditions, the operation has scaled to supply the highly sought-after premium Japanese fruit to the European market.

"We offset the high costs of materials and labor with low electricity bills. The abundant resources are expanding the possibilities for agriculture," says Noda.

Iceland's population of just 380,000 helps it meet most household electricity and heating need with massive, concentrated natural power. Japan, with a population over 120 million, requires far more power and faces geographic, regulatory and industrial roadblocks.

Japan is heavily reliant on liquefied natural gas imports and coal to generate electricity, but it boasts the world's third-largest geothermal resources (over 20 million kilowatts). However, geothermal power accounts for only 0.3 percent of its total electricity generation.

Since the devastating earthquake and meltdown of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear complex in March 2011, reductions in nuclear energy generation forced Japan to rely even more on imported LNG and coal, increasing the base cost of generation.

According to Our World in Data, Japan's per capita electricity generation from fossil fuels, nuclear and renewables in 2025 was 67 percent, 9.1 percent and 24 percent, respectively.

Because it lacks fossil fuel resources and imports the vast majority of its energy, Japan's utility costs are highly dependent on global commodity cycles and exchange rate fluctuations.

However, huge initial investments, concerns about landscape destruction, and fears of hot spring depletion have long been barriers to geothermal power development in the nation.

Many promising geothermal resources are concentrated in mountainous areas of Japan or are located within highly regulated zones such as national parks and hot spring resorts. Without drilling, it is impossible to know whether sufficient hot water is present. This uncertainty is a factor driving up costs.

Japan's deeply rooted onsen hot springs industry fiercely lobbies against geothermal development due to fears that tapping geothermal reservoirs will drain the shallow water-bearing permeable rock sediments that supply traditional bathhouses.

Nevertheless, since the March 2011 nuclear disaster in northeastern Japan, geothermal energy has still been regarded as the "last frontier" of renewable energy, according to a Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry official. Development of such next-generation technologies is afoot.

Even without hot springs, power can be generated by injecting water into high-temperature bedrock, and expectations for this new technology are rising.

Pipelines stretching across lava plateaus and EV charging stations lining city streets. This Icelandic landscape, which "which harnesses its natural resources, could serve as a model for Japan's energy strategy going forward.

New analysis of public testimony during hearings highlights health, environmental and energy-cost concerns surrounding the proposed Foundry Ridge and Red Oak Ridge plants

MILWAUKEE – Invenergy is planning to build two expensive new methane gas plants to power data centers in Wisconsin, with the goal of selling them to We Energies, despite the health, environmental and energy-cost consequences for Wisconsin communities. The two proposed gas plants in southeastern Wisconsin – the Foundry Ridge project in Darien, Wisconsin (Docket 9835-CE-100) and the Red Oak Ridge project proposal in Paris, Wisconsin (Docket 9837-CE-100) – represent a massive expansion of methane gas infrastructure to serve rapid data center development in Wisconsin.

New analysis of public comments submitted to the Public Service Commission (PSC) found that a majority of comments opposed both proposed gas plants. During the PSC hearings, 82% of speakers opposed the Foundry Ridge plant, while 88% opposed the Red Oak Ridge plant. Speakers raised concerns about higher energy costs, air and water pollution, public health risks and the burden the projects would place on nearby communities. Environmental, public health and community groups highlighted the findings during a virtual press briefing today and urged the PSC to deny both proposals.

“Building two new very expensive methane gas plants to serve Big Tech’s data centers is a step backward and Wisconsin can’t afford it,” said Cassie Steiner, senior campaign coordinator at Sierra Club Wisconsin. “Our communities showed up to testify and made it clear these projects would put their pocketbooks, air, water and health at risk.”

Advocates and subject matter experts raised concerns about gaps in Wisconsin’s regulatory review process for gas plants tied to data center development, citing a recent policy brief from the Union of Concerned Scientists. The report details how the current process of approving power plants, which considers the developer’s and utility’s applications separately, creates a loophole that restricts the PSC’s ability to weigh public concern against the plants’ harmful impacts.

“Wisconsin’s fragmented regulatory framework isolates decision-making at the expense of customers, restricting the PSC’s ability to consider public concern about the harmful impacts of new fossil gas plants,” said Maria Fernanda Chavez, senior energy analyst at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “Utilities are circumventing the public need to give Big Tech the ability to pollute the air without being held accountable. Wisconsin needs community-driven solutions that bolster a cleaner and more affordable energy future. Commissioners and elected officials must prioritize energy policy that puts people above profits.”

These proposals are part of an expanding pipeline of gas plants intended to meet the rapidly increasing demand of hyperscale data centers. We Energies is taking advantage of data centers coming to Wisconsin to expand its fossil fuel infrastructure, which worsens our air, harms our health and raises our energy bills, as explored in a new report by Healthy Climate Wisconsin.

Wisconsin needs an integrated resource planning requirement and a strong clean energy standard so rising electricity demand is evaluated comprehensively, and met with the lowest-cost, cleanest clean energy resources.

The Clean Economy Coalition of Wisconsin is a group of climate, energy, environmental justice and conservation organizations, businesses and allies. The Coalition leverages the combined strength of its members to enhance the quality of life for all Wisconsinites by accelerating the state’s transformation to a clean energy economy. We believe that an economy-wide approach to decarbonization will take our state further, faster – with better outcomes for us all. We champion equity-first policies that create jobs for Wisconsin workers, build healthier communities and protect our natural resources. By working together, we advocate for clean energy solutions that work for all of Wisconsin’s diverse cultures, communities and geographies. Learn more at www.cleaneconomywi.com.

The Power Wisconsin Forward campaign is organized on the foundational truth that methane gas infrastructure is bad for our people, planet and pocketbooks. Supported by the Clean Economy Coalition of Wisconsin (CECW) and its more than 50 partner organizations, the campaign is focused on educating Wisconsinites and activating change to enable a cleaner energy future for our state that creates jobs, builds energy reliability and saves people money.

title: Column: Wildfires will worsen until US stops ignoring the climate crisis - The Virginian-Pilot
description:
But here’s the thing: Demanding compensation while gutting climate policy is asking Canada to put out the fires while Washington keeps adding more fuel.
The result will be high greenhouse gas emissions, a faster-warming climate and more summers filled with wildfire smoke blanketing the skies.
The members of Congress who wrote the letter to Canada voted for policies that are making the smoke problem worse.
But forest management alone cannot address the hotter, drier conditions that are making fires more intense and more difficult to control — that requires confronting the underlying crisis.
In 2023, more than 120 million Americans were exposed to wildfire smoke for prolonged periods.
text:
President Donald Trump argued last month that Canada should pay damages — or face additional tariffs — for the wildfire smoke recently “poisoning” American air, and claimed that he strong-armed Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during the World Cup final in New Jersey, telling Carney he needed to stop the fires.

To Trump and the Michigan members of Congress who recently declared in a letter that their “patience has run out” with Canada over the wildfire smoke: I get where you’re coming from. As a Canadian, I’d love nothing more than to stop the haze drifting over the border. The air is thick, the sunsets are unsettling and your constituents — just like ours — are coughing through summers that are no longer what they used to be.

But here’s the thing: Demanding compensation while gutting climate policy is asking Canada to put out the fires while Washington keeps adding more fuel.

The smoke blanketing part of the U.S. isn’t just a forest management problem. It’s a climate problem. Canada’s 2023 wildfire season was the worst in our history, with more than 45 million acres burned — an area considerably larger than Michigan. And by July 17 of this year, another 5.9 million acres of land was lost to fire.

Yet Washington continues to dismantle previous efforts by the U.S. government to tackle climate change. Trump and his team have rolled back clean energy initiatives, weakened environmental review and loosened critical methane regulations. The administration is even paying companies to dismantle massive wind turbine projects that would have delivered clean energy to millions, all in the name of a Luddite ideology that makes life on our planet less tenable.

The result will be high greenhouse gas emissions, a faster-warming climate and more summers filled with wildfire smoke blanketing the skies. The changes under Trump are political choices that will increase emissions and lock in new fossil fuel infrastructure, making the conditions that drive today’s severe wildfire seasons that much worse.

Trump is now threatening Canada with tariffs and demanding damages for pollution while his administration expands the industry principally responsible for heating the planet. The members of Congress who wrote the letter to Canada voted for policies that are making the smoke problem worse. The audacity is stunning.

The letter points to shortcomings in Canada’s forest management, and argues that Canada has underinvested in thinning forests, fuel reduction, prescribed burns and enforcement against arson. Canada should certainly do more to prevent and fight wildfires. More than 5,300 firefighters were battling the fires, and Canada should commit additional funding to preventing these blazes before they start.

But forest management alone cannot address the hotter, drier conditions that are making fires more intense and more difficult to control — that requires confronting the underlying crisis. The atmosphere does not recognize borders. It makes little difference whether the pollution comes from Texas, Pennsylvania or Alberta. It contributes to the same warming that dries forests and intensifies fires across the continent.

Wildfires are also one of North America’s fastest-growing public health threats. The smoke now choking the air contains PM2.5 particles — tiny pollutants that can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, raising the risk of asthma and serious cardiovascular disease, while contributing to premature death. In 2023, more than 120 million Americans were exposed to wildfire smoke for prolonged periods. Children, seniors and people with preexisting health conditions are especially vulnerable.

An angry letter won’t protect those communities. You need policies that cut emissions through a shift to cleaner energy while helping communities adapt to what’s now an annual crisis.

The smoke drifting south may come from Canadian forests — but the political winds making it worse are coming from Washington. Unless the United States changes course, next summer will probably look just like this one. Or worse.

To the people of the United States: If you’re tired of breathing wildfire smoke every summer while lawmakers blame Canada instead of tackling climate change, speak up. Demand an end to new fossil fuel projects.

Unless we dramatically reduce emissions, the smoke will keep coming — every summer, every year. And no tariff will stop it.

Felix Horne is a senior expert with Climate Rights International based in Ottawa. He wrote this for the Los Angeles Times.

title: I Build AI Data Centers. I Want Them to Disappear From View. - Business Insider
description:
For most of my career, when asked, I told people I built data centers.
Contrast that with today and how often I get calls and see texts asking this and that about data centers.
Data centers went from large concrete buildings assumed to be just another warehouse to headline news.
Innovation was all about making data centers less resource intensive, faster to build, and modular so they would come together like Lego bricks.
Data centers need to fade into the background too, and that is the goal of every data center designer.
text:
This first-person essay was written by Sean James, a distinguished engineer in energy systems at Nvidia, where he works on the power and energy infrastructure needed to support AI data centers. He previously spent more than two decades at Microsoft designing and building data centers.

Chances are you passed an electrical substation today that delivers power to thousands of homes at hundreds of thousands of volts. It was so unremarkable that you didn't even notice. Sometime in the past, these marvels of engineering simply vanished into the background.

For most of my career, when asked, I told people I built data centers. And only in the last five years did people know what one even was. I still don't think my mom knows what I do. Contrast that with today and how often I get calls and see texts asking this and that about data centers. Mostly, it's questions about water usage and energy demand. Data centers went from large concrete buildings assumed to be just another warehouse to headline news. And I want them to disappear again.

I recently left Microsoft where I spent 25 years operating, designing, building, and toward the end, innovation. Innovation was all about making data centers less resource intensive, faster to build, and modular so they would come together like Lego bricks. Last month, while cleaning out my home office, I came across a page of notes from 2015. Scrawled across the top: Top 3 Career Goals. One of them read: disappear the data center. This remains the goal.

"The most profound technologies are those that disappear." - Mark, Weiser, Scientific American, September 1991. Disappearing tech can still be seen; I am not talking about hiding it. Technology matures until it blends into daily life and stops asking for attention. It becomes unremarkable. Like water mains and substations, infrastructure graduates when it stops being news, stops demanding attention from us. Two decades ago, our focus was to keep data centers invisible by making sure they were always online and powered up and never the source of an outage.

Now think of a data center like a factory. An industrial engineer's job is to identify and kill all non-value-added parts. A slug of steel goes in one end, and a wheel comes out the other end, and the mission is to make everything in the middle as elegant, fast, and efficient as possible. The AI factory works the same way, turning electricity into tokens.

Unfortunately, data centers are not disappearing today. I would not want to live next to one. Loud, dust, traffic, water, interactions with the grid. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) issued a rare Level 3 alert in May, its highest tier. The trigger: events where more than 1,000 megawatts of data center load dropped off the grid in seconds. Voltage dips are common on the grid, and we don't even notice them in our homes. But data centers are designed to protect their servers. When they sense a dip, they let go of the grid and jump to onsite batteries. The computers ride through without a blink. The grid takes the hit. This type of disappearing makes our grid unstable.

Believe me or don't, but I have watched the data center diminish over the decades. Energy needed to cool servers dropped when evaporative cooling replaced chillers. Server companies keep relaxing temperature requirements to make servers easier to cool. PUE, the measure of how energy efficient a data center is, has gone from 3 to 5 in the 90s to 1.2 to 1.5 today. Waste, too. I remember mountains of foam from server packaging. Now racks arrive fully assembled in reusable wooden boxes. Safety at data center projects has become the highest priority. Workers go home whole and projects are uneventful. And those of us who design them are still not satisfied. Chasing the next breakthrough is what gets us out of bed in the morning.

Today, the data center is starting to vanish one piece at a time.

Nvidia, where I work now, went public this summer with a design that runs coolant at up to 113 degrees, hotter than a hot tub. At that temperature, heat exchangers and outside air can carry the heat away in most climates. No cooling towers. Cooling water use at the site drops to zero. Data centers are also learning to be grid assets instead of liabilities. Grid stabilizers. Flexing to hand capacity back when the grid is stressed. Riding through voltage dips instead of letting go. Even the diesel generators are starting to disappear from the design, replaced by fault-tolerant networks, batteries, and fuel cells.

The criticism of data centers is important feedback. A lot of it is accurate. Some of it is not. The encouraging part for me is to see the open dialog. Data center designers can't improve in a vacuum. And the local jurisdictions that set the rules for construction need to modernize them, so that development of any kind meets the needs of the communities that host it.

Substations and water towers are critical to modern life. They surround us, quietly hidden in plain sight. Data centers need to fade into the background too, and that is the goal of every data center designer. We will continue to make them efficient, sustainable, and eventually unremarkable.

text:
For the last few weeks, we’ve been running a sidebar survey how (or if) Electrek readers think the first Chinese electric cars will make it onto US roads. After receiving more than 3,000 responses, here’s what you told us.

In case you missed the survey, the question read, “With Canada’s new canola for cars deal bringing Chinese EVs to North America, it’s not a matter of IF but WHEN they’ll arrive in the US … how will the first Chinese EVs be sold in the US?”

Given the thousands of Chinese electric cars already making their way into Canada, and the growing list of legacy brands (both American and European) working closely to develop new electric vehicle platforms with the Chinese, it seemed to me to be a matter of when, not if, Chinese EVs would come to the US. Nearly 1 in 5 of you disagreed.

By the numbers

With nearly 500 votes, the “It’ll never happen – the feds will lock down the borders if it means protecting the US’ auto industry,” crowd seemed convinced that the Feds wouldn’t let it happen. Interestingly, however, they didn’t seem to think it mattered which set of Feds we were talking about.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

I think both major parties consider China a “threat” and therefore will continue to block any sales with bipartisan enthusiasm. Perhaps the only way this changes is if China decides to really play hardball w rare earth metal sakes to US and forces a trade deal.

DAVID JOHNSON

Still, the majority of responders seemed to agree that the Chinese were coming, with nearly 700 people agreeing with “my” vote: that GM, Ford, or Chrysler (Stellantis) will bring them in under a JV and sell them through dealers, sort of like Geo or Eagle did in the 1980s.

If you look at how the Japanese automakers came to the US. Typically a importer takes and interest creates “brand of America” then sells the cars. It happened with motorcycles as well. It’s already happened with Chinese motorcycles.

[Malcolm] Bricklin brought in Subaru founding “Subaru of America” he was going to bring in Chery cars to the us 20 years ago. But it didn’t work out.

MRVC

My favorite comment, however, was about Ford’s Chinese connection with its luxury brand, Lincoln – a brand that I (and maybe some of you) consistently forget still exists.

Ford is already importing Chinese vehicles and selling them as “Lincolns”.

MARK HORNING

Mark’s right. Ford builds its Lincoln Nautilus at Changan Ford’s Hangzhou plant in China, with Ford’s own technical specifications identifying the Hangzhou facility as the vehicle’s final assembly location and NHTSA explicitly lists the Nautilus’ assembly plant as Hangzhou, China. In other words: one of America’s most historic domestic brands is already selling a Chinese car in the US.

That’s not new, either. Volvo has imported Chinese-built cars since 2015 and Honda’s most recent Fit was imported into North America (Canada) from China – and that’s not counting the “banned for being Chinese” Polestar EVs, which are Swedish-designed that are actually made in the USA in South Carolina, but nothing makes sense anymore so it’s fine.

Right? Head on down to the comments and let us know what you think of these results – and be sure to vote in the next one!

title: No More Asphalt Shingles: This Eco-Friendly Roofing Alternative Is Gaining Popularity
description:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) estimates that asphalt shingles alone create over 13 million tons of construction and demolition debris annually.
The eco-friendly roofing choice currently winning this race is metal roofing, according to Oren Levy, the founder of Gesh Group.
Elaborating on why homeowners are shifting away from asphalt shingles in his exclusive interview with Hunker, Levy states, "Asphalt shingles don't last as long and usually end up in landfills when they're replaced."
Other than fire resistance, some homeowners are favoring metal over asphalt shingles for its durability and low maintenance.
But if you aren't too keen on getting metal roofing, there are other eco-friendly roofing materials that you can explore.
text:
Asphalt shingles have dominated American roofs — and landfills — for years. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) estimates that asphalt shingles alone create over 13 million tons of construction and demolition debris annually. And it arrived at this data point nearly a decade ago in 2015! But with climate concerns mounting and landfill square footage shrinking, many homeowners are looking for roofing alternatives that won't be as damaging to the environment. The eco-friendly roofing choice currently winning this race is metal roofing, according to Oren Levy, the founder of Gesh Group.

Elaborating on why homeowners are shifting away from asphalt shingles in his exclusive interview with Hunker, Levy states, "Asphalt shingles don't last as long and usually end up in landfills when they're replaced." Indeed, BASF conducted a study which found that over 35% of roofers were concerned about their environmental impact. As they rarely last beyond 20 years, they require frequent replacements, though the worst parts are that they're rarely recycled and may even contain formaldehyde. Moreover, notes Levy, "They can also create runoff as they break down over time, which is why you see LID plans to retain water on site." LID, or low impact development plans, involve practices designed to retain stormwater rather than channeling it away through pipes.

Metal roofs, in contrast, have an average life of 40 to 70 years. So, they're more sustainable, delay replacements by decades, and are fully recyclable. "Metal roofs last much longer, can often be recycled, and are a more environmentally friendly choice overall," asserts our experts.

Read more: Is Burning A Tree Stump A Good Idea?

Why are metal roofs becoming popular

Touching on their popularity, Levy mentioned experiencing a noticeable upsurge in clientele for metal roofing as a countermeasure against fire risk. "We're seeing more homeowners choose metal roofs, especially in areas where wildfires are a concern," he states. "One of the biggest benefits is that metal is noncombustible, so it offers better fire protection."

Other than fire resistance, some homeowners are favoring metal over asphalt shingles for its durability and low maintenance. "It also lasts a long time, requires very little maintenance, and has a clean, modern look," he adds. Additionally, it's known to handle moisture better, which may be useful in stormy areas, though be prepared for a dent or two if an errant tree branch falls over your roof. Those experiencing hot climates, especially with poorly-insulated homes, may also find metal roofs useful to save money on air conditioning. Metal reflects sunlight and its heat away from your roof, keeping the area relatively cooler. For this reason, EnergyStar and the EPA consider metal as a cool roof material. Brownie points if it's coated in light colors or reflective paint.

But to take advantage of these benefits, metal roofs should be installed properly. Unlike asphalt shingled roofs that can be installed in two days or less, metal roofs demand more skill because the installers must ensure proper alignment, fastening, and sealing, often using specialized equipment. Otherwise, their performance will be compromised. Other hidden disadvantages to metal roofing that you should know about are that they can be noisy during a heavy downpour or hailstorm and are generally expensive upfront.

Which metal roof should you go for and other sustainable choices

Out of different types of metal roofs, Levy makes the case for standing seam during his interview with Hunker. "I usually recommend standing seam metal roofing. It has a clean, timeless look, performs really well, and works on both modern and more traditional homes," he says. Often made of galvanized or stainless steel, aluminum, or copper, a standing seam metal roof offers the distinct advantage that all fasteners are hidden from plain sight, thus weaving a seamless, integrated unit. However, it doesn't get boring, as the seams are arranged in different ribbed or striated styles and often stand a bit higher than the main panel.

But if you aren't too keen on getting metal roofing, there are other eco-friendly roofing materials that you can explore. "Clay tile, concrete tile, and slate are all great options because they last for decades," says Levy. Well-maintained, they may hold strong for over 100 years and may be even more sustainable should you select reclaimed variants. "If the budget allows, solar roofing is another good option that can help reduce energy costs over time," he adds. By enrolling in net metering arrangements and state incentive programs, you might recoup the full cost in about 15 years or less.

Their success helped transform Germany into Europe’s largest economy and made the country synonymous with automotive manufacturing.
The market that once generated extraordinary profits has evolved into one where German manufacturers must fight simply to maintain relevance.

The future of the global automotive industry will likely be determined by adaptability rather than legacy.
text:
For decades, Germany’s automotive industry stood as one of the world’s premier symbols of industrial excellence. Brands such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW built global reputations on engineering precision, premium quality and technological innovation. Their success helped transform Germany into Europe’s largest economy and made the country synonymous with automotive manufacturing.

Today, however, that foundation is under unprecedented strain. A combination of slowing global demand, intensifying competition from Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufacturers, rising production costs, geopolitical tensions and shifting consumer preferences has pushed Germany’s leading automakers into one of the most challenging periods in their modern history.

The difficulties confronting German manufacturers extend far beyond Europe. They offer an important case study for automakers worldwide-including those in the United States-as the global automotive market undergoes its most significant transformation in decades.

For many years, China represented the growth engine of Germany’s luxury automobile industry. Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW generated substantial profits by expanding aggressively into the Chinese market through partnerships with local manufacturers. Rising incomes and rapid urbanization created enormous demand for premium vehicles, allowing German companies to dominate many market segments.

That relationship has changed dramatically.

Chinese automakers, once viewed primarily as low-cost producers, have invested heavily in research and development, battery technology, software integration and advanced manufacturing. Supported by years of industrial investment and the world’s largest EV supply chain, companies such as BYD, Geely and others have become formidable global competitors.

As a result, German brands have experienced sharp declines in Chinese sales. Consumers increasingly choose domestic brands that offer competitive technology, sophisticated digital features and lower prices. The market that once generated extraordinary profits has evolved into one where German manufacturers must fight simply to maintain relevance.

This reversal illustrates how quickly industrial leadership can shift when technological disruption combines with strategic government investment.

The transformation from internal combustion engines to electric mobility represents perhaps the greatest challenge the global automotive industry has faced since its inception.

German manufacturers invested billions of euros in electrification while simultaneously maintaining traditional vehicle production. Managing both systems has proven extraordinarily expensive.

Unlike previous technological shifts, electric vehicles require entirely different supply chains. Batteries now account for a significant portion of vehicle costs, while software increasingly determines customer experience. These are areas where Chinese manufacturers have developed considerable advantages through years of investment.

Meanwhile, many European consumers have adopted electric vehicles more slowly than policymakers anticipated. Higher purchase prices, concerns over charging infrastructure and uncertainty regarding resale values have contributed to softer-than-expected demand.

The mismatch between ambitious production targets and actual consumer demand has left several manufacturers struggling with excess capacity and declining profitability.

Germany’s automotive sector also faces internal challenges unrelated to technology.

High labor costs, complex regulatory requirements and lengthy product development cycles have reduced flexibility. While these characteristics historically supported exceptional quality and worker protections, they can also slow adaptation during periods of rapid technological change.

Chinese manufacturers often introduce entirely new vehicle models within eighteen months. Many traditional Western manufacturers typically require considerably longer development timelines, making it difficult to respond quickly to changing consumer preferences or emerging technologies.

At the same time, energy prices in Europe remain elevated compared with several competing manufacturing regions, increasing production costs further.

Industry executives have therefore begun discussing factory restructuring, workforce reductions and production optimization as they seek to restore competitiveness.

The automotive industry is no longer divided primarily by geography. Competition now revolves around technology ecosystems.

Success increasingly depends upon battery chemistry, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving capabilities, software updates and digital services alongside traditional engineering.

Chinese manufacturers have demonstrated impressive capabilities across many of these areas. Their domestic market provides enormous production volumes that help lower manufacturing costs while accelerating innovation cycles.

This combination of scale and technological progress has enabled Chinese companies to expand rapidly into international markets across Asia, Latin America, the Middle East and parts of Europe.

As these companies gain experience and strengthen their brands, competition is expected to intensify further.

Although the United States remains protected from large-scale Chinese vehicle imports through tariffs and trade restrictions, American manufacturers cannot assume they are insulated from global competitive pressures.

Ford, General Motors and other automakers face many of the same structural challenges confronting their German counterparts.

Electric vehicle development requires enormous capital investment while profitability remains uncertain. Consumers continue to show strong interest in pickups, SUVs and hybrid vehicles even as manufacturers invest heavily in fully electric platforms.

At the same time, many battery materials, electronic components and critical minerals continue to originate from supply chains concentrated in Asia.

Industry leaders have acknowledged these realities. Ford Chief Executive Jim Farley has repeatedly warned that Chinese manufacturers represent one of the industry’s greatest long-term competitive challenges, emphasizing that American companies must prepare for an increasingly competitive global marketplace.

Whether Chinese automakers eventually enter the US market directly or expand through manufacturing partnerships elsewhere in North America, competitive pressure is likely to increase over time.

Public policy has played an important role in shaping the automotive transition.

Governments across Europe and North America introduced subsidies, tax incentives and emissions regulations designed to accelerate electric vehicle adoption and reduce carbon emissions.

Supporters argue these measures are necessary to address climate change and encourage technological innovation.

Critics contend that rapid regulatory changes have sometimes outpaced consumer demand and imposed substantial costs on manufacturers during an already challenging technological transition.

Regardless of one’s perspective, policy decisions continue to influence investment strategies, production planning and consumer purchasing behavior.

Manufacturers therefore face the difficult task of adapting not only to technological disruption but also to evolving regulatory environments.

Despite current challenges, neither German nor American automakers should be underestimated.

German manufacturers retain globally recognized brands, extensive engineering expertise and loyal customer bases. Their reputation for safety, driving dynamics and premium craftsmanship continues to attract millions of buyers worldwide.

Similarly, American manufacturers possess significant strengths.

Pickup trucks and large SUVs remain highly profitable segments where Detroit companies maintain strong brand loyalty. Established dealer networks, extensive manufacturing experience and decades of customer relationships provide meaningful competitive advantages.

Hybrid technology may also offer an important bridge between conventional internal combustion engines and fully electric vehicles, particularly in markets where charging infrastructure remains limited.

The future of the global automotive industry will likely be determined by adaptability rather than legacy.

Manufacturers capable of combining advanced software, competitive battery technology, efficient manufacturing and strong brand identity will be best positioned to succeed.

Those relying primarily on historical reputation may find themselves losing market share to newer competitors that innovate more rapidly and produce vehicles more efficiently.

Germany’s experience demonstrates that even world-leading industrial champions are not immune to disruption. Companies that dominated global markets for generations can quickly face significant competitive challenges when technological change accelerates.

For Detroit, the message is not one of inevitable decline but of urgent preparation.

The American automotive industry still possesses substantial strengths, including engineering talent, manufacturing expertise and globally recognized brands. However, maintaining those advantages will require continuous innovation, investment in next-generation technologies and careful management of evolving global supply chains.

The transformation currently unfolding in Germany is therefore more than a European industrial story. It is a reminder that leadership in the automotive sector is no longer guaranteed by history alone.

As competition intensifies and technology reshapes transportation, every major automaker-whether in Germany, the United States, Japan or South Korea-must continuously reinvent itself. Those that adapt successfully will define the next era of mobility, while those that fail to evolve risk seeing decades of industrial leadership steadily eroded in an increasingly competitive global marketplace.

Director of Transportation Tom Vander Woude is leading the transportation plan work, which is underway.

text:
The Northwestern Indiana Regional Planning Commission is seeking the public’s help in shaping the region’s future.

NIRPC is updating its NWI 2050+ plan, which sets goals to accomplish by the year 2050.

A survey seeking feedback for the plan is live at nirpc.org.

The agency has been at various events, including the Porter County Fair. It also plans a pop-up event at the Lake County Fair.

Director of Environmental Programs Kathy Luther walked NIRPC’s Environmental Committee through the process Thursday.

NIRPC is gathering public input and stakeholder feedback through November. Then begins work on plan recommendations, including updating the Transportation Improvement Plan, which looks at major road and transit projects in Lake, Porter and LaPorte counties and identifies funding for them. The transportation plan sets a timeline for which projects will be funded when, to keep planning and construction on track.

Director of Transportation Tom Vander Woude is leading the transportation plan work, which is underway.

In some areas, NIPRC’s transportation, economic development and environment focus areas intersect.

“There is extensive emphasis on transit-oriented development,” Luther said.

With the South Shore Line’s Double Track NWI and Monon Corridor projects up and running, there are transit development districts around train stations intended to promote transit-oriented development.

In Hammond, The Banc is an apartment building, having converted the former Calumet Bank building downtown into residential use. The downtown train station within easy walking distance is expected to be completed next year.

In Michigan City, a symbiotic residential building is attached to the 11th Street Station. The Franklin is expected to be ready for occupancy soon.

Those are two examples of what transit-oriented development aims to accomplish.

Many of the goals of the existing NWI 2050+ plan will remain the same, but others are being updated to reflect progress already made.

One goal deals with communities adopting climate action plans. Gary already has one in place. Greenhouse gas inventories are already completed for all three counties and 15 municipalities, so NIRPC’s share of the work is completed, with local government expected to do the rest of the work.

Luther shared a draft of the climate and environment section.

“In going through the worksheet, I’ve identified some strategy gaps,” she said.

“There’s nothing in there specific to brownfields, although there are things in there about infill and development,” Luther said.

Notably, the Northwest Indiana Regional Development Commission recently set up the Local Development Entity, which is hiring a director to lead the LDE in addressing those issues. The LDE aims to help assemble parcels for redevelopment and help identify funding for cleaning up environmental issues as well as ownership tangles.

Among the other NWI 2050+ goals is to have 95% of the NWI fleet be electric vehicles by 2050. Accomplishing that requires adding EV charging stations at public facilities, increasing the number and percentage of EVs in municipal fleets and boosting the number of EV public transit vehicles.

Drive Clean Indiana is working to help municipalities find funding for vehicles with cleaner emissions.

The existing NWI 2050+ is online at nirpc.org. The revised version will be ready for another round of public comments next spring.

Doug Ross is a freelance reporter for the Post-Tribune.

text:
A new Amazon data center is set to become the single largest source of environmental pollution in the U.S., according to a New York Times report on August 8. The tech giant — which already operates the most data centers worldwide — is reportedly building a natural gas power plant in Pecos County, Texas, to power its new data center at the same site. According to project permits, the plant would generate up to 7.65 gigawatts of power using 35 natural gas turbines. The new plant — which burns natural gas to generate electricity — has been authorized to release 33 million tons of CO₂ annually, more planet-warming gases than any other power plant in the country, says the NY Times report.

Conversely, Amazon had pledged to achieve net-zero carbon emissions across all its global business operations by 2040. The company made the promise in 2019 when it initiated and co-founded The Climate Pledge — a voluntary coalition of over 700 companies and partners — aimed at addressing its own corporate footprint and rallying global supply chains. However, the company has seen its emissions rise each year for the past several years, something analysts attribute to a spike in data centers to support the AI boom. The company is currently building several additional AI data centers globally, including the one that the new gas plant would power in Texas.

Amazon has acknowledged the impact of its intense AI ambitions on its earlier climate pledges but insisted the company remained committed to them, despite obvious struggles. “The world looks different now than when we co-founded the climate pledge,” said Margaret Callahan, an Amazon spokeswoman. Still, “our commitment hasn’t changed,” she said, echoing similar statements by Microsoft, which is struggling to fulfill its 2030 sustainability promise amid carbon-heavy AI expansion, but insists it remains committed to it.

Latest Videos FromTom's Hardware

As detailed in our data center power roadmap, an increasing number of hyperscalers and data center operators are switching from grid connections to dedicated on-site power generation. The “behind-the-meter” moves are being triggered mainly by the long timelines required to set up new power infrastructure to connect new power-hungry data centers to the grid, but also by growing anti-data center sentiments over irreversible hikes in the electricity bills of nearby communities.

While many companies are also pursuing nuclear and renewable energy options — examples being Microsoft’s Three Mile Island nuclear deal and Meta’s agreement to secure up to 1GW of orbital solar energy capacity — gas appears to be the leading preference due to its scalability and speed of availability. The Trump administration has thrown its weight behind such projects for data centers, promoting oil, natural gas, and coal over renewable energy sources.

title: Hopes grow for higher ethanol blend with inclusion in US Senate farm bill - Mitchell Republic
description:
Supporters of year-round E15 availability say it would strengthen the farm economy and make the country more energy independent.
Without a law authorizing year-round E15, summertime sales require a federal waiver .
The farm bill is multi-year legislation that determines federal agriculture, food and nutrition policies.
The Senate Agriculture Committee included year-round E15 when it released its version of the farm bill last week ahead of the committee’s hearing this Thursday.
The last farm bill was signed into law in 2018 and has been extended after Congress failed to pass a new version.
text:
South Dakota’s congressional delegation is hopeful that year-round, nationwide approval of E15 — a gasoline blend with 15% ethanol — will clear Congress this year, bolstered by its inclusion in the latest Senate version of the farm bill.

Ethanol is a fuel additive made primarily from corn, and a lower E10 blend is already available year-round. Supporters of year-round E15 availability say it would strengthen the farm economy and make the country more energy independent. Without a law authorizing year-round E15, summertime sales require a federal waiver .

Opponents point to research showing emissions from higher blends could worsen summer smog while encouraging the conversion of grasslands for corn farming. Some lawmakers from oil-producing and refining states also oppose the expansion.

The House pulled year-round E15 from its version of the farm bill earlier this year, instead approving it as separate legislation amending the Clean Air Act.

The farm bill is multi-year legislation that determines federal agriculture, food and nutrition policies. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, voted in favor of both bills.

The Senate Agriculture Committee included year-round E15 when it released its version of the farm bill last week ahead of the committee’s hearing this Thursday. The House’s standalone E15 bill awaits a hearing in another Senate committee.

The last farm bill was signed into law in 2018 and has been extended after Congress failed to pass a new version. Johnson spoke to South Dakota Searchlight on Wednesday at the Sioux Empire Fair in Sioux Falls about the legislation’s progress, including the Senate version.

“In general, I don’t think the House is going to love this version compared to what we passed, but at some point we’ll figure out a way to get to yes, collectively,” Johnson said. “We need to. This is really important if we care about American energy dominance, and we just can’t get there without E15.”

Year-round E15 sales have been a longstanding goal of the ethanol industry. Ethanol plants process more than half of South Dakota-grown corn.

Rising gas prices this summer and the ongoing war with Iran have drawn attention to the United States’ continued reliance on liquid fuels in cars and airplanes — and its entanglement in Middle East oil markets, Johnson said.

“I would rather wake up every morning worried about the price of corn in a South Dakota field than worried about the price of oil in an Iranian oil field,” said Johnson, who will leave Congress in January after his failed run for governor .

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, said in a statement that year-round E15 is a boost for agriculture and rural communities across South Dakota and the country.

“I remain committed to getting the farm bill and E15 to the president’s desk to secure these critical wins for South Dakota’s farmers and ranchers,” Thune said.

South Dakota Republican Sen. Mike Rounds has also spoken in support of year-round E15.

title: ABB Invests In LevelTen Energy To Expand Clean Energy Procurement Services
description:
ABB has formed a strategic partnership and made a minority investment in LevelTen Energy, a clean energy transaction marketplace, to expand ABB’s capabilities in renewable energy procurement and energy and carbon advisory services.
LevelTen Energy has facilitated more than 20 GW of clean energy transactions across more than 35 markets in North America and Europe.
As companies pursue decarbonization goals, large-scale clean energy procurement often requires long-term renewable energy agreements that can be complex to identify, structure and execute.
ABB also pointed to its recent investment in Gridcog as part of a broader strategy to expand capabilities across energy procurement, energy advisory, and energy and carbon services.
LevelTen Energy was founded in 2016 and provides transaction infrastructure connecting utility-scale clean energy buyers and sellers.
text:
ABB has formed a strategic partnership and made a minority investment in LevelTen Energy, a clean energy transaction marketplace, to expand ABB’s capabilities in renewable energy procurement and energy and carbon advisory services. Financial terms of the investment were not disclosed.

LevelTen Energy has facilitated more than 20 GW of clean energy transactions across more than 35 markets in North America and Europe. Its marketplace supports transactions including power purchase agreements, capacity, powered land, energy attribute certificates, energy storage agreements and granular certificates.

The partnership combines ABB’s expertise in electrification, digital solutions and energy management with LevelTen’s clean energy procurement and transaction platform.

ABB said the relationship will allow it to provide customers with a broader set of services spanning energy procurement, electrification, optimization, emissions reduction and ongoing reporting.

The companies are targeting commercial and industrial customers seeking to secure long-term clean electricity while managing energy costs and maintaining reliable operations.

As companies pursue decarbonization goals, large-scale clean energy procurement often requires long-term renewable energy agreements that can be complex to identify, structure and execute.

ABB said LevelTen fills a gap in its current offering by providing customers with a way to identify and secure clean energy through long-term agreements.

The partnership also comes as companies increasingly move beyond annual renewable energy matching toward requirements that more closely align when and where electricity is consumed with when and where clean energy is generated.

Meeting those requirements can involve technologies such as battery energy storage systems, microgrids and advanced energy management platforms.

ABB has existing capabilities in those areas, while LevelTen provides clean energy contracting and environmental attribute certificate trading. The companies believe combining these capabilities can help customers develop more comprehensive and verifiable energy transition strategies.

ABB will also gain access to LevelTen’s ecosystem of clean energy developers and projects. The company expects this to create additional opportunities to provide monitoring, optimization and lifecycle services.

LevelTen, meanwhile, is expected to gain access to ABB’s global customer relationships and domain expertise across manufacturing, industrial and commercial markets.

ABB said its presence in regions including Asia-Pacific could also create opportunities to expand the partnership into additional growth markets.

The investment was made through ABB Electrification Ventures, the venture capital arm of ABB’s Electrification business.

Including LevelTen, ABB Electrification Ventures has invested more than $110 million across 18 startups since 2021.

The unit operates within ABB Ventures, the company’s broader corporate venture capital platform. ABB Ventures has invested more than $500 million in startups since its formation in 2010, focusing on companies aligned with ABB’s electrification, automation and motion businesses.

ABB also pointed to its recent investment in Gridcog as part of a broader strategy to expand capabilities across energy procurement, energy advisory, and energy and carbon services.

LevelTen Energy was founded in 2016 and provides transaction infrastructure connecting utility-scale clean energy buyers and sellers. In addition to its marketplace, the company offers transaction tools, market intelligence software and energy market data.

KEY QUOTES:

“Our customers are under real pressure to reduce their carbon footprint while managing energy costs and maintaining reliable, 24/7 operations. One important piece missing from the solutions we provide today: a straightforward way to secure long-term clean energy at the right price. LevelTen Energy brings exactly that capability.”

“Through the partnership, ABB will be able to extend its growing energy and carbon advisory services portfolio with renewable energy procurement capabilities, helping customers move from planning and implementation to ongoing optimization and reporting.”

Stuart Thompson, President of Electrification Service Division at ABB

“The partnership is expected to accelerate growth opportunities for both companies. ABB will gain access to LevelTen’s extensive ecosystem of clean energy developers and projects, creating new opportunities to deliver monitoring, optimization and lifecycle services.”

Stuart Thompson, President of Electrification Service Division at ABB

“This strategic partnership will generate new clean energy solutions, allowing ABB’s global customers to seamlessly tap into clean power, capacity, and portfolio management tools. Together, we have a real opportunity to help even more customers decarbonize.”

That's why bladeless turbines developed by Spanish company Vortex Bladeless have the potential to be real game changers that make wind energy more widespread with less environmental impact.
Bladeless turbines can alleviate some of the current disadvantages of wind energy, the most obvious being the noise, aesthetics, and danger to birds and bats.
All of those advantages are great, but there is one big downside to bladeless wind turbines: They don't produce nearly as much energy.
Currently, Vortex Bladeless' larger turbines only produce up to 100 watts, which is significantly lower than the several megawatts that conventional wind turbines can generate.

text:
Wind is currently the most common source of renewable energy, accounting for around 10% of all electricity produced in the U.S. in 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. However, generating wind energy famously involves massive turbines with spinning blades that, while efficient, can be incredibly disruptive to people and wildlife living near wind farms. That's why bladeless turbines developed by Spanish company Vortex Bladeless have the potential to be real game changers that make wind energy more widespread with less environmental impact.

Vortex Bladeless' website breaks down how these innovative turbines work. Rather than having blades that spin with the wind, these are composed of a base and a long cylindrical post that has a carbon rod in the center. While the base is anchored to the ground, the post sways back and forth as wind flows through it, creating pressure that can be converted into electricity.

Bladeless turbines can alleviate some of the current disadvantages of wind energy, the most obvious being the noise, aesthetics, and danger to birds and bats. The biggest advantage, though, is that these turbines could be installed in cities where wind speeds are often inconsistent and unpredictable. Bladed turbines need average wind speeds of at least 9 mph or 13 mph depending on size, which is why so much wind energy comes from Texas, California, and Midwestern states like Iowa, but bladeless turbines only need around 7 mph.

All of those advantages are great, but there is one big downside to bladeless wind turbines: They don't produce nearly as much energy. Currently, Vortex Bladeless' larger turbines only produce up to 100 watts, which is significantly lower than the several megawatts that conventional wind turbines can generate. That's because, while the compactness of bladeless turbines is one of their selling points, size does matter when it comes to turbines, and bigger turbines harness far more electricity.

Vortex Bladeless is designing larger turbine models that could have an output of up to 1 kilowatt, but even that's not nearly enough to replace bladed turbines to power the electrical grid. After all, as bladeless turbines get better, traditional ones will too. Innovations that address problems with existing and new bladed turbines, such as painting a single blade black to prevent bird collisions, are still crucial, as are more ambitious projects like China's flying wind turbine.

Where bladeless turbines can really make a difference is within cities and other places that aren't suitable for large turbines or solar panels. Making renewables more accessible is an overlooked part of the green energy transition necessary to fight climate change, and bladeless wind turbines look to be a big step in the right direction.

description:
California's battery energy storage resources now exceed 21,000 megawatts, making the state’s battery fleet one of the largest in the world.

Newsom highlighted the battery storage milestone Friday as he unveiled a new ZEV rebate program aimed at lowering costs for Californians.
